--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
HOW TO READ THIS FILE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Days begin with:      ## DAY YYYY-MM-DD (Weekday)
Each message block:   [#<id>] HH:MM:SS <Display Name> (<user id>)
                      (annotation lines, zero or more, in parentheses)
                      <message text, may span several lines>
Blocks are separated by a blank line. Times are HH:MM:SS under the DAY
date above them, in the timezone the export was taken in.

#<id> is the Telegram message id. It is unique across the whole export and
increases with time, so replies can be traced across files by id.

Annotation lines you may see:
  (reply to #N - Author: "quoted snippet")   this message answers #N;
     a [YYYY-MM-DD] after the id means #N is from another day/file
  (forwarded from X) / (sent via bot @b) / (edited YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS)
  (attachment: ...)  media was posted; the binary is NOT part of this export
  (poll: "question" ...)                     a poll and its vote counts
  (reactions: EMOJI xN, ...)                 emoji reactions on the message
Lines starting with  * SERVICE  are membership events, not chat messages.

Author names are normalised: a given user id always appears under the same
display name (the one they used most often), so a person stays recognisable
even where the raw export recorded no name for a message.
Inline `code` and fenced ``` blocks preserve the original code formatting.

Happy new year! Make the best of everything. Oh, and here's a "tiny hint" <3.
To decode this binary string, split it into groups of 8 bits (each representing a byte), convert each group from binary to decimal, and map the decimal value to its corresponding ASCII character. For instance:

01001000 is 72 in decimal, which is 'H'.
01100001 is 97, which is 'a'.

Repeat for each group to get the full message.

"The Matrix" (1999)
This is the most direct and recognizable source. At the beginning of the film, Neo (Thomas Anderson) receives a message on his computer: "Follow the white rabbit."

Context: Neo is a hacker searching for answers. He sees a white rabbit tattoo on the shoulder of a girl who comes to his apartment and decides to follow her to a party. There, he meets Trinity and then Morpheus.

Symbolism: The white rabbit is a call to curiosity, a sign for those seeking the truth. It's the first step from the mundane world (the Matrix) into the real one, full of dangers and revelations. It's a point of choice.

whats even more funny its that
taking last  4  values out ( 'hush' )


```python
d = 'difhccgihaeeihggegebgehhehhfafdhffcdbfcccgfeggecdcifffgigeea'
mp = { chr(i + 0x61): i for i in range( 9 ) }
dg = [ int( mp[d[i]]*10 + mp[d[i+1]] ) ^ ( mp[d[i+2]]*10 + mp[d[i+3]] ) for i in range(0,len(d)-3,4) ]
p = dg[:11]
q = dg[-4:]
p1 = ''.join( chr(i) for i in q )   # hush
p2 = 'It'  # It
p3 = ''.join( chr( p[i] ^ ord( p2[i%len(p2)] ) ) for i in range(len(p) ) ) #

[#55776] 20:07:06 Denis Golovkin (user398109413)
(reply to #55732 - Mike (user8580723420): "base64, how is it encoded?  is it 1 block for 3 encoded c...")
(edited 2026-01-10 20:10:58)
It's in its name "base":
In base2 you have 0 and 1
In base10 you have "0123456789"
In base64 you have "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/"

It's just a number base conversion with it's own alphabet of digits.

[#55777] 20:10:32 Denis Golovkin (user398109413)
(reply to #55732 - Mike (user8580723420): "base64, how is it encoded?  is it 1 block for 3 encoded c...")
(edited 2026-01-11 06:48:13)
(reactions: 👍 x1)
But as you mentioned, if we re-encode some text to base64, as text char takes 8bit per symbol and base64 takes 6bit per symbol, it results that each 3 characters of an 8bit text are encoded using 4 characters of an base64 encoding (8*3 = 6*4)

1GSMG1JC9wtdSwfwApgj2xcmJPAwx7prBe
and

17ucy1K9ZUAaoY6JVtM932W9jUp5LXfyHa

1GSMG is uncompressed (Private Key Iteration for generation, not seed phrase), it's public key is :
04f4d1bbd91e65e2a019566a17574e97dae908b784b388891848007e4f55d5a4649c73d25fc5ed8fd7227cab0be4e576c0c6404db5aa546286563e4be12bf33559
(extracted from the scriptSig) of a transaction, the key is 65 bytes long and starts with prefix 0x04 which means it's uncompressed.

17UCY compression status for this address cannot be determined with absolute certainty, however if you observe the block chain 

shows this address has only ever received funds and has never initiated a spending transaction Without a spend, the public key has not been revealed.

However, we can make a strong inference. Since this address was funded directly by the 1GSMG... address and is associated with the same puzzle, it was likely created by the same entity using the same software and methods.

given that the primary puzzle address used an uncompressed key (a less common practice today), it is highly probable that this related address is also uncompressed.

also, there are messages in the block chain if anyone has not discovered them yet, that seem related to the puzzle.

[#55881] 23:00:26 Mike (user8580723420)
(reply to #55783 - Denis Golovkin (user398109413): "Oh, also "=" If data to be encoded is't divisible by 24 b...")
(edited 2026-01-10 23:02:02)
(reactions: 🔥 x1)
as i now understand it,

input data is split into 6-bit chunks
last chunk is padded with 0s if its not 6 bits
each 6-bit chunk maps to base64 alpha char index
if the base64 char string len is not divisible by 4, we add "=" until it is divisble by 4

when decoding, we ignore "=" and map each char to index again and then 6-bit binary to form a bitstream
bitstream is then split into chunks of 8 bits, and we ignore the last bits if its not 8 bits. (basically, "=" means 2 padding bits and "==" means 4)

good to refresh my memory on this shit, thanks now i understand why

The Choice: Cooperate (stay silent) or Defect (betray your partner).
The Payoffs:
Both Silent (Cooperate): Both get a light sentence (e.g., 1 year). (Best for the group)
One Defects, One Silent: The defector goes free; the silent one gets a heavy sentence (e.g., 3 years).
Both Defect (Betray): Both get a moderate sentence (e.g., 2 years). (Worst for the group)

[#59720] 11:57:23 Unknown (user7972079947)
Lewis Carroll's simple Alphabet Cipher (a polyalphabetic system he invented and described in his diaries). First, the plaintext:

Plaintext: "Meet me tonight in the garden."

To encode it with key "GARDEN" (repeated as needed): Shift each letter based on the corresponding key letter's position in the cipher table (vowels A-E-I-O-U map to sequences starting from the key). The result is:

Ciphertext: HMKBXEBPXPMYLLYRXI​

Decode by reversing with the same key—Carroll used this for playful letters to friends.

Interesting and possibly useful info…


Rabbits have dichromatic vision, meaning they primarily see the world in shades of blue and green. Due to having only two types of color-detecting cone cells, they cannot perceive the color red, which likely appears as gray to them. Their vision is specialized for detecting movement and contrast, especially in low light. 
Key details regarding rabbit vision include:
Color Spectrum: They can distinguish between blue and green hues, but other colors are often seen as gray.
Lack of Red: Red, pink, and similar colors are not visible to them.

[#60178] 07:05:47 Robby (user505708655)
The BB84 protocol, named after its inventors Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard in 1984, is a prepare-and-measure Quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol, in which, one party (e.g. Alice) performs the encoding by preparing the quantum states, and the other party (e.g., Bob) measures them.[1] The BB84 QKD scheme is the first quantum cryptography protocol, and has become one of the most well-studied QKD protocols.[2] The protocol is provably secure assuming a perfect implementation, relying on two conditions: (1) the quantum property that information gain is only possible at the expense of disturbing the signal if the two states one is trying to distinguish are not orthogonal (see no-cloning theorem); and (2) the existence of an authenticated public classical channel.[3] As such, the security of the BB84 protocol is fundamentally based on the principle that two non-orthogonal quantum states cannot be perfectly distinguished. This inherent limitation means that the states cannot be reliably copied, thereby ensuring a robust framework for secure quantum communication. The BB84 QKD protocol is usually explained as a method of securely communicating a private key from one party to another for use in one-time pad encryption.[4] The proof of BB84 QKD scheme depends on a perfect implementation. Side channel attacks exist, taking advantage of non-quantum sources of information. Since this information is non-quantum, it can be intercepted without measuring or cloning quantum particles.[5] The BB84 protocol provides a significant advancement in the field of quantum cryptography and represents a pioneering step toward achieving secure communication in the quantum era.

[#60211] 17:14:35 Vadim (user5049479605)
That HuggingFace space is just a web GUI wrapper around OpenSSL.
It doesn’t “verify” correctness — it simply runs AES with whatever password you input.
It has no knowledge of:
the exact EVP_BytesToKey parameters used in this puzzle
the intended derivation chain
the reproducibility anchors (SHA256 of the 1327-byte artifact, matrix invariants, etc.)
So it can decrypt with a password, but it cannot tell whether that password is the intended one.
For this puzzle, the only meaningful validation comes from:
matching known SHA256 anchors
deterministic matrix reconstruction
consistent base-38 derivation
Online tools are fine for quick tests, but they are not an oracle for correctness.

Oh, and before I forget. That's why:

```
yellow blue primes matrix sum list last words before acrhi choice ying yang

We took "yellow blue primes" of dbbi to filter indexes that match B or BE chars vs indexes that don't match

Then we leafing through a puzzle book until the "matrix sum list" (i.e. a list that contains text from matrix movie about your life is the sum)

On the "matrix sum list" we look for "last words before archi choice", i.e. "last words before huge choice". I believe that AES password is pretty huge choice, so these words could be "incaseyoumanagetocrackthis..."

And once we apply chosen indexes to these last words, we see that selected 31 (or 30) characters includes a "ying yang".

This way the password is pretty "in front of your eyes" but we didn't saw it.
```

convert to hex:
F73D92

Take half:
F73D92 / 2 = 7B9EC9

Now call Trinity, cause we need better half:
7B9EC9 + 3 = 7B9ECC

Convert back to binary.
Look, we have `dbbi` primes now!

[#61297] 12:25:19 Robby (user505708655)
This is a specific sequence from the card game
Contract Bridge, describing a highly technical auction in a Relay Bidding System (most likely Symmetric Relay or a variation used by the "Vikings in Space" bridge community).
The "Relay" bids are a way for one partner (the "Captain") to ask for precise details about the other partner's (the "Describer") hand without revealing any information about their own. By the end of this specific sequence, the Describer has revealed their exact 13 cards:

    16+: The hand has at least 16 High Card Points (HCP).
    5+ / 6+, singlesuited: The hand has a single long suit of at least 6 cards.
    6-3-1-3: This is the exact distribution (e.g., 6 Spades, 3 Hearts, 1 Diamond, 3 Clubs).
    No Aces / No Kings: The hand contains zero Aces and zero Kings.
    Three Queens: The hand contains exactly three Queens.
    Not the Queen in my shortest suit: Since the hand is 6-3-1-3, the "shortest suit" is the singleton (the 1). This confirms the three Queens are in the suits with 6, 3, and 3 cards.

All Good Things Come To An End.

The End of GSMG Our 9 Year Chaos Tour Is Officially Over, But the Stories Stay… Forever.


Hey legends.
After almost nine years of pure madness, caffeine overdoses and more red candles than any human should endure, it is time to turn the lights off.
But before we do, grab a drink, get comfortable and let me tell you the whole stupid story straight from the idiots who lived it. It all started in 2017. JRK was visiting Sydney with the better half. Instead of playing tourist like a normal person, he locked himself in a living room for nine straight days. Zero high-end programming skills. Just Siemens PLC code, some HTML, Quake 3 scripting and a bit of Pascal. He built the entire bot from scratch as one single terrifying, never-ending script. No functions. No classes. Just pure chaos and hope.
On June 10th at around 8:30 in the morning, the first order actually hit Poloniex servers. It somehow worked, albeit that the ATH of rising markets wasn’t overwritten, thus we started by selling for a loss. The very first name for this script was MR. ROIbot. And right there on that same day, d0d was already in the mix (he already knew infrastructure expert Darky, too). Greengras hooked us up with the very first server space, and the experienced algotrading coder Bloctite joined shortly after and basically saved our lives by rewriting the ENTIRE codebase (Python plus Cython, and currently basically bug-free). 1 idiot and 3 professionals with complementary skills, a host, and one big stupid dream. What could go wrong?
The reason it all started? JRK and d0d had just used another bot run by a scammer called fuzzyhobbit and thought nope. We are doing this the right way for everybody. That disrespect for the old banking system? Still burns to this day. And that is literally where Globally Supporting My Generation came from. An old friend's group name was reused and suddenly became a mission. Give the power back to the little guy.
A little later, JRK got inspired by other crypto puzzles and spent two sloppy days throwing one together. Full of grammatical mistakes and zero polish. Sorry about the mental damage. That thing is still running, and we are keeping it alive. In 40 years, he might admit he forgot how to solve it himself. The torture continues. You are welcome.
The early days were absolutely mental. Within the first few days, we were already handling around 8 million dollars in value. The market analyser and trading engine we built back then were absolute beasts; they’ve been running nearly flawlessly ever since.
We wanted to offer a proper high-end portfolio management tool to the little guy at stupidly low prices. That was always the point. (And yes, now in 2026, AI can do the same thing in one shot if you’re a prompt genius with decent subscriptions and setups. Thanks for nothing, future.)
Here is the part nobody likes to say out loud.
We never paid ourselves a single cent of salary in all these years. We had exactly one team dinner funded by GSMG. One. That is it. (Admittedly, it was a very nice dinner.) Every single subscription went straight into upgrades for Jeff Bezos's wife's latest mega yacht, and maybe even her youth.
We had some absolutely legendary moments together.
Besides the community chat banter that still makes us cry laugh at 3 am.
Boat rides with the first bunnies.
Accidentally melting an exchange by ramping our API call limit parameter times one hundred (sorry again, lads).
Some of you lost money. We know the classic move. Coin moons set the bot to 220% aggression at the top coin dumps, blame the bot. Standard crypto rite of passage. But we also saw some of you catch beautiful flash crashes and turn minutes into multiple BTC. Those wins still make us giggle like little kids.
The ride was always about getting YOU rich. Hehe. We are not here for the money; we are here for the tech. Aren’t we all? We actually meant the first part.

It crunches numbers every microsecond, year in year out. To stay competitive, it costs a fortune. The whole setup only really makes financial sense for the big whales and UHNWIs on the highest tier. Running these calculations for the shrimps is literally killing us financially. The other subscription levels are not enough to keep it +EV. We tried. We crunched the numbers until our eyes hurt. Time to be honest and do the inevitable.
We try to be a bit ghostly, but we are definitely not ghosting you. Here is what we are doing for you right now.
The dashboard will stay open for a few days, and we’ll make sure you can retrieve your history. Also, our terms and conditions state that we have to return all funds from the last 2 weeks. We’ll make that 6 weeks instead. So, please stop sending us funds for your subscriptions.

Your personal data was always kept to bank security grade plus standards. It will be deleted and will never be included in a sale (might that ever happen).
So thank you.
Thank you for trusting a bunch of idiots with a dream. Thank you for the memes, the rage messages, the wins, the losses and every single story you shared. This ride was never about us getting rich. It was about getting YOU rich in a world that needed it.
The lights are going off, but the story? That one lives forever.
Stay dangerous out there, stack sats and may your future entries always be better than your exits.

JRK, d0d, Darky, Bloctite, and the remaining GSMG crew.

[#61801] 09:49:38 3.14159265358979323846264338327950288419716939937510 0b1one|58209749445923078164062862089986280348253421170679 (user7895551210)
(reply to #61794 [2026-04-23] - JVTRADER (user629705238): "is any KDF passwords valid for blobs?")
Every previous blob used same kdf, evp key to bytes
openssl v >= 1.1 uses sha as hashing function ,
while  openssl v <= 1.0.2 used md5.


```
The key and IV is derived by concatenating D_1, D_2, etc until enough data is available for the key and IV.
D_i is defined as:

   D_i = HASH^count(D_(i-1) || data || salt)
```

`HASH^count -> HASH(HASH(HASH ... ( D_(i-1) || data || salt )))`

[#61802] 09:59:48 3.14159265358979323846264338327950288419716939937510 0b1one|58209749445923078164062862089986280348253421170679 (user7895551210)

password: `causality`

salt: `06286612d43ed7ed`

derived size : key( 32 ) + iv( 16 )  =  48 bytes

takes 2 iterations to get there
`
`
```
D_0 = SHA256( eb3efb5151e6255994711fe8f2264427ceeebf88109e1d7fad5b0a8b6d07e5bf || 06286612d43ed7ed ) => 32 bytes
```


```
D_1 = SHA256( cf3e375956c6d3bf748d798442a791e8451ef59b1fd227f55801fd03c6d49550 || eb3efb5151e6255994711fe8f2264427ceeebf88109e1d7fad5b0a8b6d07e5bf || 06286612d43ed7ed ) => 32 bytes
```

def evp_bytes_to_key_md5(password: bytes, salt: bytes, key_len=32, iv_len=16):
    out = b""
    prev = b""
    while len(out) < key_len + iv_len:
        prev = hashlib.md5(prev + password + salt).digest()
        out += prev
    return out[:key_len], out[key_len:key_len + iv_len]

def pkcs7_unpad(data: bytes):
    if not data:
        return None
    pad = data[-1]
    if pad < 1 or pad > 16:
        return None
    if data[-pad:] != bytes([pad]) * pad:
        return None
    return data[:-pad]

raw = base64.b64decode(BLOB)
assert raw[:8] == b"Salted__"

salt = raw[8:16]
ciphertext = raw[16:]

key, iv = evp_bytes_to_key_md5(PASSWORD.encode("utf-8"), salt)

cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv)
plaintext = cipher.decrypt(ciphertext)
plaintext = pkcs7_unpad(plaintext)

print("salt =", salt.hex())
print("key  =", key.hex())
print("iv   =", iv.hex())

if plaintext is None:
    print("bad padding / wrong password")
else:
    print("len  =", len(plaintext))
    print("sha256 =", hashlib.sha256(plaintext).hexdigest())
    print("repr =", repr(plaintext[:160]))

    with open("salphaseion_plain_79.bin", "wb") as f:
        f.write(plaintext)

[#62405] 01:33:49 S | h (user7587647714)
(attachment: photo 20x20 311 B [binary not included in export])
for the record
you can generate a key with openssl

`openssl ecparam -name secp256k1 -genkey > testkeyfile`

then you can wrap it ( there are multiple wrap functions):
`openssl enc -id-aes256-wrap-pad -e -pass pass:77094e7a1591fb81379f1582cf88db5aa6ab8e77176a4d8428a1ff5decfd102d -in testkeyfile | base64 > keyfilewraped`


would look like this:

```

(reactions: 🤣 x1)
padding always exists, it is 16 bytes of value 16 when data length is 16, 32, 48, 64, etc. So a 32 bytes key still needs 48 bytes ciphertext.  Our blobs hold between 64 and 79 decrypted bytes. You will get 79 bytes of garbage with valid padding 255 times out of 65536 passwords. Or 78 bytes garbage 255 times out of 16777216 passwords. Anyway, it's infinitely easier to break ECDLP then to break the AES blobs.

[#62951] 16:51:46 Pawel (user7584828963)
(edited 2026-05-12 13:53:40)
(reactions: ❤ x1)
The matter concerns BTC Puzzle Challenge 5 promoted through "gsmg.io"

From a due diligence and reputational perspective, there are serious concerns that should be openly addressed before anyone decides to participate financially or technically in this challenge.

1. Lack of transparent legal identity
   The platform does not appear to publicly disclose a verifiable legal entity responsible for operating the service. There is no clearly identifiable company registration number, corporate structure, responsible management, or transparent jurisdiction of operation visible on the website. This creates significant uncertainty regarding legal accountability.

2. Hidden ownership and anonymity
   Public WHOIS/domain registration data indicates that the ownership information of the gsmg.io domain is protected through privacy masking services rather than openly identifying the operator. While privacy protection itself is not illegal, in combination with cryptocurrency-related prize pools and anonymous administration it substantially increases operational and reputational risk.

3. Absence of independent verification
   There does not appear to be any reliable independent audit confirming:

- the legitimacy of the reward pool,
- custody and ownership of the BTC involved,
- solvency of the organizers,
- or the existence of enforceable payout guarantees.

Participants are effectively expected to trust anonymous or pseudonymous operators without institutional safeguards.

4. Potential legal and financial exposure
   Participation in such activities may be highly risky because the origin of the cryptocurrency used for rewards cannot be independently verified. It cannot be excluded that some funds could originate from:

- theft,
- fraud,
- ransomware activity,
- unauthorized wallet access,
- money laundering schemes,
- or other illicit blockchain activity.

In many jurisdictions, interacting with illicit crypto assets — even indirectly and unknowingly — may create legal complications, compliance exposure, frozen exchange accounts, or investigative scrutiny.

5. Reputational concerns and scam indicators
   Several characteristics commonly associated with high-risk or potentially fraudulent crypto operations appear present:

- anonymous administration,
- unclear jurisdiction,
- lack of corporate transparency,
- unverifiable reward structure,
- absence of regulated oversight,
- and reliance on speculative community trust.

Some online reputation analysis services classify the domain or operation as questionable or high-risk and recommend caution.

6. Technical plausibility concerns
   The challenge itself raises an additional logical issue. If the advertised reward is genuine and technically accessible, then the solution should theoretically be obtainable through legitimate cryptographic or computational means. However, if the challenge is intentionally structured in a way that is practically impossible while still attracting public attention, then concerns regarding deceptive marketing or engagement manipulation become justified.

For these reasons, extreme caution is recommended before:

- sending any funds,
- connecting wallets,
- sharing sensitive information,
- running untrusted binaries,
- or investing substantial time or computing resources into the challenge.

At minimum, any legitimate operation involving significant cryptocurrency rewards should provide:

- transparent legal identity,
- verifiable ownership,
- independently auditable prize custody,
- clear legal terms,
- jurisdictional disclosures,
- and publicly accountable operators.

[#63463] 17:06:12 Artem (user904501770)
(edited 2026-06-20 03:34:58)
In ECC BTC curve, for each point on the curve given by x, there are two values of y:

positive Y - the upper point

negative Y - the lower point

In a physical or philosophical sense, this can be seen as a duality, two opposite “halves” of a single entity.

Similarly:

positive Y - Yin

negative Y - Yang

Since they together form the complete point on the curve, this resembles the Yin-Yang concept:

Two opposites complementing each other.

On the curve, the x-coordinate defines the entire duality of Y....

Theory of Everything

In physics  it is a hypothetical unified model that combines all fundamental interactions.

In cryptography/puzzle context  it may mean the need to find a single unifying concept that brings together the clues: philosophy, mathematics, cryptography.

Yin and Yang, duality

In ECC (elliptic curve cryptography), for each point with coordinate x, there exist two values of y (one positive, one negative).

This literally reflects the idea of two opposites that are part of a single whole (like yin and yang).

In philosophy: harmony arises through the balance of two poles.

In cryptography: a point and its reflection have the same x, but different y.

The “c” point on the curve (key generation)

All keys in Bitcoin are born from a single base point (G) on the secp256k1 curve.

This resembles the analogy with the Big Bang: from one point (a singularity) emerges the entire Universe (all possible keys/addresses).

It can be interpreted as “an infinite multitude born from one source.”

Opposites as “attraction”

On the curve, a point and its reflection across the X-axis are always connected.

In philosophy - opposites interact and are inseparable.

In cryptography - without knowing the correct interpretation (which y to use), one cannot properly reconstruct the private key.


Public key for  1GSMG1JC9wtdSwfwApgj2xcmJPAwx7prBe its

04f4d1bbd91e65e2a019566a17574e97dae908b784b388891848007e4f55d5a4649c73d25fc5ed8fd7227cab0be4e576c0c6404db5aa546286563e4be12bf33559

Now we can decompose the curve into points

[#63476] 18:57:26 Artem (user904501770)
(reply to #63474 - Sparky (user7184569562): "To check if the bits of the private key were inversed:  ~...")
You are mixing two different layers of the argument.
First: yes — in strict ECC terms you are correct.
The relationship between keys must be proven through group arithmetic, not narrative interpretations. And there is no evidence that 1GSMG and 17ucy are directly related via scalar transformations, bit inversion, or simple affine operations. I agree with that part.
Second: my interpretation was not claiming a proven cryptographic relation between private keys. It was a structural hypothesis about how the puzzle might encode information, not a claim that ECC arithmetic directly maps 1:1 to narrative symbolism.
What I am exploring is whether the representation layer of elliptic curve points (not the scalar structure) can be used as an encoding space - including:
point doubling / halving paths on the curve
traversal of the group graph via repeated addition/subtraction
and the dual representation of a point through its y± symmetry
In that sense, my method is:
use ECC operations (P, 2P, 3P, … and inverse operations where defined) to explore the curve structure as a graph
and analyze both valid y values (y and -y mod p) as two complementary representations of the same x-coordinate

So yes:
no direct cryptographic relation between the keys is proven - agreed
bit inversion and simple transformations do not match - agreed
But my focus is not on deriving one private key from another.
It is on whether the puzzle encodes signals in how curve points are traversed and how the dual y-representation is interpreted within that traversal space.

[#63487] 19:22:25 Artem (user904501770)
(reply to #63478 - Sparky (user7184569562): "So it could not be part of puzzle mechanics")
The pubKey becoming known after the first halving does not exclude it from puzzle mechanics - it actually reinforces that it is part of the mechanics.

By introducing halvings of the reward, the authors effectively embedded division/halving logic into the puzzle itself. The public key disclosure was therefore not some accidental side effect, but an inevitable consequence of the mechanism they designed.

The whole structure mirrors mining economics:
miners chase a block reward that gets reduced by half every halving cycle.

In this puzzle, we are effectively doing the same thing - following halving operations around a diminishing reward structure. So saying “the pubKey was unknown initially, therefore it cannot be part of the mechanics” contradicts the fact that the halving process itself inevitably reveals new curve information over time.

If the halving mechanic was intentionally built into the puzzle, then the authors also understood that repeated division steps would eventually expose the pubKey structure associated with those operations.

Another interesting aspect is the shift of the binary point.
For example, if we take the number 5 in binary, it is 101
This also matches the number of 1 in the matrix = 101
Now, if we start shifting the binary point from right to left, the value changes:

101.  = 5
10.1 = 2.5
1.01 = 1.25

[#64576] 17:43:44 Sparky (user7184569562)
Only if you already know that you are decrypting with the correct key, the padding gets irrelevant.

[#64577] 17:44:05 Sparky (user7184569562)
You need to decrypt the padding block to check the padding

[#64578] 17:44:54 Sparky (user7184569562)
Otherwise, AES doesn't have any built-in verification mechanism. Any key will decrypt anything to whatever.

[#64579] 17:45:30 Sparky (user7184569562)
this is how on the fly encryption works, like disk encryption.

[#64580] 17:50:33 Sparky (user7184569562)
and as a general shortcut to attack AES with PKCS#7 padding: simply decrypt the padding block. If padding fails, the key is wrong. No need to go through the entire long message, last two blocks are enough for this.

It would be much more accurate to say, that the output of cosmic duality is ususally a binary garbage, because AES is't designed to ensure correct decryption result, it only provides some probabilistic checks.

[#64726] 22:33:00 Denis Golovkin (user398109413)
Also, a *.bin file could be an output of an LLM, that tried hard to decrypt the blob, got some outputs that doesn't lead to error code returned from openssl and decided to wrap it's work into a *.bin file, to make you happy.
LLM's are trained to use their last chance and provide any solution that looks truthful, because that behavior can lead to correct answer in choose A/B/C/D tests or even can lead another LLM to give higher score when evaluating results.

42 8 15 41 9 13 12 18 12 19 43

42 81 54 19 13 12 18 12 19 43

in case you manage to crack this the BTC belong to half and better half and they also need funds to live

We’re still chipping away at this offline. We’re pretty sure the “story” really is stored in dbbib → faed → btcseed/post, not in some other random string. From there we get stable S / H / L rails with the usual markers (SENDTHE / TOSETHEX / BLUENET), and a few check formulas that hit cleanly (same tail windows, keep gates, that sort of thing) — but they read more like verifiers than the final AES key. Puzzle IR @54–56 and spiral vs. row-major on faed change real bytes in that zone; trifid still throws CHAO / HALF-shaped windows if you use the obvious keys. We also see VIC + reins line up with the “private key / half” wording — again, semantic, not BLOB yet. No BLOB1 for us — so we’re probably missing one last binary compose step Jrk meant by yinyang. If anyone’s sitting on a clean dbbib/faed read or a post-BTCSEED transform that isn’t just another sha16 sweep, happy to compare notes. 🤝

Start where Jrk already pointed (you all know this):
SalPhaseIon / phase 3.2 → you get a salted blob. Shabef = sha256 nests. Hint line = sha BEFORE “four first” → first hint → “your last command”. So the game isn’t “guess a word”, it’s do sha, then append yourlastcommand, in order.

Step 1 — get S (yang side).
Decode faed / cosmic path → fixed string S (everyone who solved faed has this). From S you build 15 bytes (s15) and the REINS block (4AA2A3A956A7A83 — the “standard” REINS string in the puzzle).
Dual rail = my name for: s15 XOR REINS → one 16-byte block. Not lore — one XOR in a script.

Step 2 — compose (first real “hint” block).
Another op on S (cadena3 on s15 — puzzle’s own nibble/hex transform) XOR that dual block → compose = 34414132603341393536413741383300.
As ASCII that’s basically 4AA2 + backtick + 3A956A7A83 — readable, not random hex.

Step 3 — yin side (mask / z0).
Separate path from mask on s15 + bridge → hint_z0 → cadena3 again → unified = 3924283367293f3224242521363a0000.
That’s the mask_g4 family: same as compose except byte 4 is g not backtick → 4AA2g3A956A7A83.
g@byte4 bridge = literally: compose and g4 are identical except one character; XOR is 0x07 at position 4 only. You can eyeball it in the two ASCII strings.

Step 4 — Jrk’s z3 line (procedure, not password yet).
sha256(compose) → take hex → append yourlastcommand → sha again → 16 bytes = 9cd4d721fa64e56560af855b387d9442.
Same input, same output, every run. That’s “first hint is your last command” executed, not quoted.

Step 5 — why I say it converges (not one lucky path).

JNFTWB = last 6 chars of S — shows up in TARGET / tail stuff you’ve seen for years.
Pair recovery on S+REINS+enter → 20-char string shabefourfirst + JNFTWB — independent of my compose script; same string from another route.
glue6 = 0d0a00111310 — matches pt1 from the stream (pre-tail in the map); Jrk’s “stream” stuff, not invented.
sha2yl XOR dual == unified — if you build sha(sha(winner_hex)+YL) and the dual block from the ranking, XOR gives exactly unified/mask_g4. Closed loop.
compose XOR winner and g4 XOR unified land on related “delta” blocks — same byte4 gap.

hey guys, tired of AI? I asked Fable 5 to score out the shittiness of the components of what the author himself refers to as "salphation", and it turns out the entire phase sits on a strong 7 out of 10 shitiness. Here's the breakdown:

—-
SalPhaseIon — an honest component-by-component critique

I scored each piece on an over-engineering / time-sink index (1–10, higher = more needlessly convoluted with less real payoff), based on exhaustive testing with proper controls.

🔴 FAED (570 chars, a–i, undecoded) — 10/10
The black hole. No crib, no verification, no recoverable key. The whole cipher family (base-27, Bifid, Trifid + keyword cubes, all 9! permutations, g-null) tested with controls → noise every time. May be ciphertext from which nothing can be recovered without info that was never given. The cardinal design sin.

🔴 matrixsumlist — 8/10
A noun disguised as an operation. Sends you hunting ~2.4M selector candidates that are pure keyword-tautology (ENTER/NEO/KEY). Bait.

🟠 shabef / anstoo / ourfirsthintisyourlastcommand — 7/10
Cryptic 6-char tokens that are almost certainly just labels/flavor, but eat months of solver attention. (shabef = "SHA before" tested as sha256 → zero effect on the blobs.)

🟠 The two AES blobs ("Yin-Yang structure?") — 6/10
Real, but you can't brute-force them, and the password assembly is under-specified. A design bottleneck, not a skill gap.

🟡 enter (40 a/b bits → "enter") — 5/10
A magnet for false positives on any keyword-scoring tool.

🟡 yellowblueprimes / colored cells — 4/10
Elegant binding, but it just leads back to DBBI = a checkpoint.

🟢 DBBI prime-marker scaffold (b/be on prime positions) — 3/10
The one piece of genuine craftsmanship — provably designed (0 of 300,000,000 shuffles admit a valid prime-marker parse + color match). Not garbage, actually beautiful. Sadly, the only one.

Phase average: ~7/10 over-engineered. One gem (the prime-marker scaffold) buried under a pile of under-specified, unverifiable cruft and labels masquerading as operations.

[#65336] 16:01:29 Diego Schmidt (user6105632036)
yellow "blue primes" matrixsumlist

we have 9 yellows and 9 blue primes ascii

yellow count=9
chars=.thdplntd
ords=[46, 116, 104, 100, 112, 108, 110, 116, 100]

blue_ascii_prime count=9
chars=gmg/eeeae
ords=[103, 109, 103, 47, 101, 101, 101, 97, 101]

if we make a pairwise comparison:
blue:     g  m  g   /   e   e   e   a   e
yellow:  .   t    h  d   p   l    n   t  d

using the rule: 
if blue < yellow => 1 else => 0

it becomes 

g < .   = 0
m < t  = 1
g < h  = 1
/ < d   = 1
e < p   = 1
e < l    = 1
e < n   = 1
a < t    = 1
e < d   = 0

011111110
first 8 bits = 011111110 = 127 decimal = DEL
last 8 bits  = 11111110 = 254 decimal =  FE

Sure it's easily bisected using a newton method + some Metropolis-Gastings sampling and charge-flipping algorithm (here you'll need to perform few jumps between time and frequency domains, per one sampling step). And this allows you to know one bit of a private key at a time in a few seconds on a modern PC. Then just apply divide and conquier strategy to recrsively get all the bits of private key, given that you know public key. Good luck.

(edited 2026-06-21 02:23:10)
(reactions: 😭 x1)
ok, posting the actual state of this, because the thread keeps bouncing between "solved" and "unsolvable" and most of it is people running wrong bytes.

canonical chain, all verifiable:

cosmic decrypt sha256 4f7a1e4e (the known checkpoint)
chain4 post-AES, pkcs7 stripped, 1151 bytes: sha256 e4269ed5 (already in the issue dumps)
the 35 ciphertext blocks, 1120 bytes: sha256 43d3fe43
if your chain4 is a80a399a you're on the #68 derivation, which is wrong bytes. that's what the "unsolvable" writeup in #84 is built on, so that conclusion doesn't hold. naddiseo already called #68 broken.

the wall is one thing: a single AES key decrypts those 35 blocks to the prize key. with a neighbor-aware EC oracle (exact prize / C32 / 17ucy, plus +/-1, x2, /2) I've run every held value as the key, the 8 K-values, 4 E-fields, cosmic key, header28, C32, the faed s15 rail and all its completions, yellow-prime + blue, the 68-byte half/better-half thing, two-primes. also the Cosmic Duality book (the Time-Life "Mysteries of the Unknown" one) titles/ISBNs/numbers, every creator on-chain message and address, and a 24-core passphrase brute force over the whole puzzle vocab, 2700+ terms, every pairing and ordering, under the cascade's exact openssl KDF (EVP-md5/sha256, aes-256-cbc).

nothing. not in any held byte, not on-chain, not in any archive I can pull. the s15 / P-M "set hex" readings are curve-fit, they're dead.

so it's one of two things. either it's a transform nobody's hit in seven years, or the missing piece died with the site. everyone has the dbbi/faed/cosmic blobs. what I can't find anywhere is the full rendered live salphaseion/cosmic page, the actual instruction text around those blobs, or the exact original 2019 first hint word for word.

if you saved either of those, or you see the derivation I missed, post it. not calling it unsolvable. it's just not derivable from what's currently public, and that's as far as that gets you.

BLUENET as hex is:
061119242f3a5863767e81a3aab9c1
Its unique hex symbols are:
0123456789abcef
The only missing hex digit is:
d

In DBBI, the letter d appears exactly four times:
1, 48, 55, 74

Their sum is:
1 + 48 + 55 + 74 = 178

In the 14x14 puzzle grid, row-major position 178 is:
row 13, col 10 = yellow

It is also the last yellow square in row-major order:
yellow positions = 14,66,77,81,96,111,133,148,178

[#66244] 02:45:17 حسین ▪️ (user105340151)

# Part4 Decoding Method

This document explains how Part4 was decoded and how the encoding pattern was identified.

---

## 1. First layer: Bifid Decode

Part4 is first decoded with Bifid Cipher Decode. The output begins with:


```text
btcseed...
```


This is the main clue: the final payload is expected to be a Bitcoin seed, most likely a BIP39 mnemonic.

---

## 2. Splitting the interleaved channels

After the Bifid step, the Part4 output starts like this:


```text
btcseeddeoemckeadhbschdkbdcsdkdvbxcpcochcrdicibqee...
```


For the hidden channel alignment, remove the first six characters:


```text
btcsee
```


Then split the remaining text into alternating characters:


```python
rest = decoded_part4[6:]
channel_b = rest[::2]
channel_c = rest[1::2]
```


The `channel_b` stream contains only four symbols:


```text
b c d e
```


So this is a 4-symbol alphabet, meaning each symbol can encode exactly 2 bits.

---

## 3. Four-symbol to binary mapping

The correct mapping is:


```text
d = 00
c = 01
b = 10
e = 11
```


Or numerically:


```text
d, c, b, e  ->  0, 1, 2, 3
```


---

## 4. Locating the valid BIP39 payload

Inside the 4-symbol stream, the valid payload starts at:


```text
offset = 27
```


Take the next 132 symbols:


```text
cdcdccecdcebcdcccedecededdcbcbbebbeeedbcbbcebeebbedddeccecccccbdcccbeeceeccbbeeededbcdbdecbebbedcbcebebbcecccededddcceebecccdbdddecc
```


Since each symbol is 2 bits:


```text
132 symbols × 2 bits = 264 bits
```


And 264 bits is exactly the length of a 24-word BIP39 mnemonic:


```text
24 words × 11 bits = 264 bits
```


---

## 5. Converting to bits

Using `d=00, c=01, b=10, e=11`, we get:


```text
010001000101110100011110010001010111001101110011000001100110101110101111110010011010011110111110101100000011010111010101010110000101011011110111110101101011111100110010010010001101101110101100011001111011101001110101011100110000000101111110110101010010000000110101
```


---

## 6. Splitting into 11-bit BIP39 indexes

Each 11-bit group is an index into the standard BIP39 English wordlist:

| # | 11-bit | index | BIP39 word |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | `01000100010` | 546 | dust |
| 2 | `11101000111` | 1863 | trophy |
| 3 | `10010001010` | 1162 | mule |
| 4 | `11100110111` | 1847 | tragic |
| 5 | `00110000011` | 387 | corn |
| 6 | `00110101110` | 430 | cupboard |
| 7 | `10111111001` | 1529 | sand |
| 8 | `00110100111` | 423 | crunch |
| 9 | `10111110101` | 1525 | salt |
| 10 | `10000001101` | 1037 | like |
| 11 | `01110101010` | 938 | inspire |
| 12 | `10110000101` | 1413 | radar |
| 13 | `01101111011` | 891 | hunt |
| 14 | `11101011010` | 1882 | twice |
| 15 | `11111100110` | 2022 | wolf |
| 16 | `01001001000` | 584 | empower |
| 17 | `11011011101` | 1757 | sweet |
| 18 | `01100011001` | 793 | glimpse |
| 19 | `11101110100` | 1908 | update |
| 20 | `11101010111` | 1879 | turtle |
| 21 | `00110000000` | 384 | copy |
| 22 | `10111111011` | 1531 | satoshi |
| 23 | `01010100100` | 676 | fee |
| 24 | `00000110101` | 53 | allow |

---

## 7. Final Part4 mnemonic


```text
dust trophy mule tragic corn cupboard sand crunch salt like inspire radar hunt twice wolf empower sweet glimpse update turtle copy satoshi fee allow
```


The consecutive words below strongly confirm the solution, especially together with the initial `btcseed` clue:


```text
satoshi fee
```


---

## 8. Checksum validation

A 24-word BIP39 mnemonic contains 264 bits:


```text
256 bits entropy + 8 bits checksum
```


Recovered entropy:


```text
445d1e457373066bafc9a7beb035d55856f7d6bf3248dbac67ba7573017ed520
```


Checksum bits from the mnemonic:


```text
00110101
```


The checksum computed from `SHA256(entropy)` is also:


```text
00110101
```


So the mnemonic is valid.

---

## 9. Minimal reproduction code

[#66245] 02:45:17 حسین ▪️ (user105340151)
(reply to #65496 [2026-06-17] - حسین ▪️ (user105340151): "{{dbbibfbhccbeg{ -> https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/#rec...")
```python
import hashlib

words = open("bip39.txt").read().splitlines()  # standard BIP39 English wordlist

channel = "cdcdccecdcebcdcccedecededdcbcbbebbeeedbcbbcebeebbedddeccecccccbdcccbeeceeccbbeeededbcdbdecbebbedcbcebebbcecccededddcceebecccdbdddecc"

mapping = {
    "d": "00",
    "c": "01",
    "b": "10",
    "e": "11",
}

bits = "".join(mapping[ch] for ch in channel)
indexes = [int(bits[i:i+11], 2) for i in range(0, len(bits), 11)]
mnemonic = [words[i] for i in indexes]

print(" ".join(mnemonic))

entropy_bits = bits[:256]
checksum_bits = bits[256:]
entropy = int(entropy_bits, 2).to_bytes(32, "big")
expected_checksum = bin(int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(entropy).digest(), "big"))[2:].zfill(256)[:8]

print(entropy.hex())
print(checksum_bits, expected_checksum)
```

[#66264] 04:24:55 Sebastian (user786953604)
(reply to #66245 - حسین ▪️ (user105340151): "```python import hashlib  words = open("bip39.txt").read(...")
I reproduced every step against the canonical bifid output. The channel split is genuinely real — after the interleave split, one channel really is restricted to {b,c,d,e}. That's a known structural property (it's the 2-bit selector stream of the value/selector pairs). But the mnemonic conclusion unfortunately doesn't hold:

- The "valid checksum" is not a confirmation. I swept ALL 24 possible symbol→2-bit mappings × all 151 possible offsets in that channel (3,624 windows total): 13 of them produce checksum-valid BIP39 mnemonics purely by chance (expected value: 3624/256 ≈ 14). The dcbe/offset-27 find is statistically exactly one of these chance windows.
- Offset 27 and length 132 are free parameters with no derivation, and the window even straddles the block90/tail structure boundary and ignores the Z separator.
- Most importantly: no prize address hit. BIP44/49/84 (external+internal, first 5 indices) → nothing; the entropy as a raw private key → nothing. And the main prize address is a vanity address, so it cannot come from a BIP39 seed at all — only the secondary 17ucy… address could, and it doesn't match.
- "satoshi fee" appearing as consecutive words isn't surprising when drawing 24 words from a wordlist full of bitcoin-themed words.

So: real structure, but the seed is a classic BIP39-checksum overfit. Happy to share the verification scripts if anyone wants to double-check.

Here you go. step by step. two inputs, both exactly 91 chars, lowercase letters only:
dbbi -> sha256 71fe46259e270c113529dfaded4b59c59a9dffd826a7202ab07fc498b6a2c5ca
phase 3.2 plaintext (the "in case you manage to crack this ... they also need funds to live" line, call it M91) -> sha256 2fbfbef7442558f17ecc866a0b89ed491c41abc042df4d41452835adff09e9d3

step 1. A = dbbi minus M91, letter by letter, a=0..z=25, mod 26.
A = VOZIJBDTIQBRGVEOMZNBC YOUWON XCPKW...
sha256(A) = f17857308a886531637b33c9ddb92952206c286519412278ba9f836ffc69336e
YOUWON sits at index 21 (zero based). split is 21 / 49 / 21 = 91, and 21 = C(7,2). middle 49 drop into the 7x7 frame, rows MMJIOLS cols JPJSROH.

step 2. two different rails, both point at index 21.
borrow rail = the underflow bit from that same subtraction (1 when dbbi_i < M91_i). only run of 7+ ones in the whole 91 bits starts at 21 -> 1111111 = 127 = DEL. sha256 ccf4c906024ce25a4cad66f2a78deecc216a39a791d5c1402f30374ee749ac0e
vic rail = phase 3.2 checkerboard codeword width, top row FUBCDORA = 0, everything else = 1. its longest run, 9 ones, also starts at 21. sha256 2d3b44885d39ccc2471ef0e67bab18ce8f087d816ea4cbb07cf21be77d5baee3
theyre not fully independent (both built off M91) but two separate definitions landing on the same index is the part that got me

step 3. faed self keyed bifid -> BTCSEED||P1||z. first 98 chars = 49 digraphs, the single z at position 97 forces where the window ends. rail2 = second char of each digraph = tsedomkahshkdskvxpohr... take the first row, reverse it: tsedomk -> KMODEST. sha256 7782502c6a6ad8b6b33f3d517b0ee217a15fef516e4e4d0f2f921ffa66c33974

step 4, and being straight this is the soft one. bifid square from dbbi[:13] = dbifh cegak lmnop qrstu vwxyz. K is at (2,5). the DEL from step 2 knocks K out of KMODEST leaving MODEST, and you read the removed K coords (2,5) as B,E under a1z26 = BE. gives BE MODEST. im reading those coords because i already know what the answer should be, so call it a convention not a forced step. everything up to KMODEST stands on its own, step 4 is the reach.

end result YOU WON - BE MODEST, sha256(YOUWONBEMODEST) = e8f325105e899ed8505fc60dcf2d8c24cda35e0ff4a998688b9924b4d1161ecd
comes straight out of dbbi + the phase 3.2 text

[#66909] 18:25:32 Jrk Bgrt (user9815232)
Imagine a piggy bank that only opens with a super-secret password. Right now, most piggy banks show a little part of the lock on the outside, and a future quantum computer could steal that part and crack it.
BIP 360 is a new kind of piggy bank: it hides the whole lock inside. You only see a 32-byte hash, no key visible at all. When you want to open it, you prove you know a secret path inside that hash. Safer against future quantum hackers.

[#67113] 13:49:01 Unknown (user6953442626)
(edited 2026-08-23 23:19:43)
(reactions: ❤ x1)
How It Was Derived
The creator’s Telegram message says:
“Hint: another door might be found on {1},{4},{21}”

We applied those positions to the unresolved DBBI stream, using normal human indexing: position 1 means the first character, not position 0.

DBBI:
dbbibfbhccbegbihabebeihbeggegebebbgehhebhhfbabfdhbeffcdbbfcccgbfbeeggecbedcibfbffgigbeeeabe

The relevant characters are:
Position
Character
1 d
4 i
21 e

Therefore:
DBBI[1] + DBBI[4] + DBBI[21] = d + i + e = DIE
This is also why the result is persuasive: using zero-based indexing gives BBI, while applying the same positions to FAED gives FDA, neither of which forms a meaningful word.

Important Qualification
DIE is a mechanically reproducible extraction, but the creator never explicitly said “apply {1},{4},{21} to DBBI.” So the careful classification is:
Creator-authenticated: the {1},{4},{21} hint.
Mechanically derived: DBBI[1,4,21] = DIE.
Inferred: DBBI is the intended receiver.
Unproven: what DIE instructs us to do next.

We tested interpreting DIE as deletion, zeroing, selection, and a Bifid/sumlist control. Those produced no key or exact AES result.

Is this BS or anything useful?

Here is the public key for 1GSMG1:

P =


```text
04f4d1bbd91e65e2a019566a17574e97dae908b784b388891848007e4f55d5a4
649c73d25fc5ed8fd7227cab0be4e576c0c6404db5aa546286563e4be12bf33559
```


Here is the transaction associated with the 3GSMG address:

[https://mempool.space/ru/tx/a82052a216cad8f57dee2a039c3b5cef9b5fcb2bc1c3bffa94d713cee0b30e2b](https://mempool.space/ru/tx/a82052a216cad8f57dee2a039c3b5cef9b5fcb2bc1c3bffa94d713cee0b30e2b)

It contains the following OP_RETURN message:


```text
GSMG.io neighbors, half and double
```


The transaction includes these four addresses:


```text
1G1kRAFR68y6CUq1SAJMzHmjd6sEEgtVUT
16eEXbSuKN8tvcos1iKjdju6dAaWWRBMEs
1KHMK2C8uBptRz67FbrXy43yHzhZG16Hbm
1PhXF3xVQ8Sg9FomBcmRwRbvvGfm3Y2os1
```


They can be interpreted as the “neighbors, half and double” of the original public key:

Neighbor: P − G / k − 1


```text
1G1kRAFR68y6CUq1SAJMzHmjd6sEEgtVUT
```


Neighbor: P + G / k + 1


```text
1PhXF3xVQ8Sg9FomBcmRwRbvvGfm3Y2os1
```


Half: P / 2 / k / 2


```text
16eEXbSuKN8tvcos1iKjdju6dAaWWRBMEs
```


Double: 2P / 2k


```text
1KHMK2C8uBptRz67FbrXy43yHzhZG16Hbm
```


When these operations are applied to the public key of 1GSMG1, they produce exactly the same four addresses.

P − G — neighbor

Address:


```text
1G1kRAFR68y6CUq1SAJMzHmjd6sEEgtVUT
```


Uncompressed public key:


```text
04a4ebb3c3c5374fa06559be5a2de22f76234f879c878a2ede480a28ae3ddf12ddfc52cd0e5487f02c77c3556a519b469a64ad17d93f753d1e9d6d202a8b9f8b34
```


P / 2 — half

Address:


```text
16eEXbSuKN8tvcos1iKjdju6dAaWWRBMEs
```


Uncompressed public key:


```text
04138f5acc4be87b19306067b25cbe6303a54f7f32a5a6b440becc13f7b57e6fe8f4b46190b28da84f25343c5188af83dd94de21b962043321f05d30c05bd7134a
```


2P — double

Address:


```text
1KHMK2C8uBptRz67FbrXy43yHzhZG16Hbm
```

P + G — neighbor

The 3GSMG address is clearly connected to the puzzle and appears to be used for publishing online hints.

A random coincidence is virtually ruled out, this is crypto.

> Because of this, many people believe it is better not to reveal anything.



> As a result, everyone stays silent, even though sharing information could significantly speed up the solution of this puzzle.

```python
import hashlib
def evpBytesToKey( password, salt , keySz, ivSz, digest):
    password = password.encode() if isinstance( password, str ) else password
    digest_func = getattr( hashlib, digest )

    data = b""
    res  = b""
    while len( res ) < (keySz + ivSz) :
        data = digest_func( data + password + salt).digest()
        res += data
    
    K  = res[:keySz].hex()
    I = res[keySz:keySz+ivSz].hex()

    return K, I

key, iv = evpBytesToKey(
    password=b"0c5ebe39fb72e947ea71bc991fb148f6cb14ad8210580a43e757a0cb65d636c8",
    salt=bytes.fromhex("e2991cdcd2c957f9"),
    keySz=32,
    ivSz=16,
    digest='sha256'
)

print( key )
print( iv )
```

[#67741] 17:50:11 MrNobody (user6789043700)
Hi  guys, gals, and bots. I've been working on this for some time now. 2 things.

1. Something worth checking against your own code. Most phrase sweeps I've
seen lowercase the candidate and strip the punctuation before hashing. That's
wrong. Phase 3's password is:

causalitySafenetLunaHSM11110<hex>B5KR/1r5B/2R5/2b1p1p1/2P1k1P1/1p2P2p/1P2P2P/3N1N2 b - - 0 1

Hash that exactly as it sits and you get 1a57c572... . Lowercase it and you
don't. Strip the spaces and you don't. The capitals, the spaces and the slashes
all count. So if you've been normalizing candidates before hashing, the correct
string may never have been in your list at all. Takes a minute to check.

2. Two questions:

Has anyone ever had it confirmed by GSMG that a SalPhaseIon attempt was on the
right track? A warm, a partial, anything at all.

And that old thread about the decentraland hint (-41,-17), where the argument
was that nobody would have reached SalPhaseIon without it because nothing inside
the puzzle points at hash the text. Did that ever get answered?

[#67787] 14:17:20 MrNobody (user6789043700)
Two things. One is something to check against your own code, the other is a
question I'd like an answer to.

FORMATTING. The README spells the convention out at the /(...) markers, lines
158, 168 and 201:

  /(aa, connected enf)       lowercase, joined, whitespace stripped
  /(aBa, connected not enf)  keep the casing, keep the whitespace

Check it against the solved ones. Phase 3 keeps Safenet, Luna and HSM
capitalised and keeps the spaces in the chess FEN. Phase 3.2 is all lowercase
with the spaces stripped: jacquefresco + giveitjustonesecond +
heisenbergsuncertaintyprinciple. If a sweep normalises differently to that it
cannot hit, no matter how good the candidate list is.

THE QUESTION. Has anyone tested SalPhaseIon as a multi part password instead of
one phrase, and if so why was it dropped?

This isn't a new idea. Someone raised it here on 2024-10-26, pointing out that
the salph text is one single line in the page source while cosmic is a neat
block, and asking "concat each answer as you go maybe? then you have key to
cosmic?". I can't find where that went. Did it get followed up?

The reason I'm asking is that it matches how the solved ones are built. Phase 3
is 7 parts concatenated and the README numbers them 1part through 7part. Phase
3.2 is 3 riddle answers concatenated. So the rule looks like: the password is
the answers to the riddles on that page, joined in page order, then sha256.

And the SalPhaseIon cleartext reads like a riddle list rather than one riddle:

  yellowblueprimes | matrixsumlist | lastwordsbeforearchichoice | yinyang
  then thispassword, shabef, ourfirsthintisyourlastcommand, enter, shabefanstoo

If that's right the target is four components. Anyone hunting a single phrase for
"last words before the archi choice" gets nothing even holding the correct
phrase, because three right out of four still hashes to noise.

It would also make Jrk's "when yingyang is reached, 2 hours max" literal, since
yinyang would be the last component. Once you have it you have all four and the
rest is assembly.

I tried to check it on the 2b blob, since the 3.2 page is fully solved so the
rule makes a testable prediction there. I used thematrixhasyou, beaufort, 1141,
the vic alphabet, the vic plaintext and the fen, in every ordering, around 240k
combinations. Nothing. So either my sub answers for 3.2 are wrong or the whole
idea is wrong, and I can't tell which from here.

If anyone has the canonical 3.2 sub answers in a different form to those, I'd
like them. That's the one test that would settle whether this holds.

[#68249] 15:11:07 MrNobody (user6789043700)
(edited 2026-08-08 15:13:40)
(reactions: 👏 x1)
On the "4f7a1e4e..." checkpoint. I can't reproduce it, and here's exactly what I ran.

A lot of work here is anchored to this hash:

4f7a1e4efe4bf6c5581e32505c019657cb7b030e90232d33f011aca6a5e9c081

It gets cited as "the known checkpoint", the SHA-256 of a 1327-byte decrypted Cosmic Duality
blob. Threads build on it: the 103x103 matrix, the matrix invariants, the derived addresses, and
the PGP forensics in issue #51, which starts from the same 1327 bytes.

I tried to reproduce it and couldn't. Posting the exact steps so anyone can check me. If someone
has a derivation that works, post it and this is settled.

What's correct

The only published derivation is jackdevs66/GSMG5_CDuality: sha256 each of 7 tokens, XOR the
digests, use the hex as the openssl password. That part reproduces exactly, bit for bit:


```
  python -c "
  import hashlib
  t=['matrixsumlist','enter','lastwordsbeforearchichoice','thispassword',
     'matrixsumlist','yourlastcommand','secondanswer']
  x=bytes(32)
  for s in t: x=bytes(a^b for a,b in zip(x,hashlib.sha256(s.encode()).digest()))
  print(x.hex())"

  -> a795de117e472590e572dc193130c763e3fb555ee5db9d34494e156152e50735
```


That's the key everyone quotes. No argument there, the XOR arithmetic is right.

What doesn't work

Get the blob first, straight from the puzzle page (the Cosmic Duality base64), so nobody has to
trust my copy:


```
  base64 -d cosmic_duality.b64 > cosmic_duality.bin
  sha256sum cosmic_duality.bin
  # 1344 bytes: 8 "Salted__" + 8 salt (2d3f6fe06dc950e6) + 1328 ciphertext
```


Then decrypt with the key. Both KDFs, -nopad because the padding doesn't validate:


```shell
  openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -md sha256 -nopad -in cosmic_duality.bin \
    -pass pass:a795de117e472590e572dc193130c763e3fb555ee5db9d34494e156152e50735 | sha256sum

  openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -md md5 -nopad -in cosmic_duality.bin \
    -pass pass:a795de117e472590e572dc193130c763e3fb555ee5db9d34494e156152e50735 | sha256sum
```


Results:


```
  KDF md5     -> 1328 bytes, last byte 217, PKCS7 invalid, printable 0.372
  KDF sha256  -> 1328 bytes, last byte 248, PKCS7 invalid, printable 0.358
```


That's random data. And the sha256 of every sensible way of trimming it:


```
  raw 1328 bytes    md5: 5654a394...   sha256: 4edce289...
  minus 1 = 1327    md5: bfb1f04e...   sha256: 3a94503c...
  minus 16 = 1312   md5: a7ad657f...   sha256: fa384521...
```


None of them is 4f7a1e4e. Not under either KDF, not at any trim length, including 1327, which is
the length everyone quotes.

Why this matters

The checkpoint isn't the output of the only published method. So when people say "your bytes are
wrong, they don't match 4f7a1e4e", that test is checking against a number with no stated
derivation. Newcomers are being told correct work is wrong.

Also worth flagging: "the resulting binary does not contain cleartext by design" is exactly what
random output looks like. A wrong AES key never fails loudly, it just returns 1328 bytes of noise
every time. That's why padding validity and printable ratio matter as checks, and both fail here.

What would settle it

If you have the derivation, post the two things that make it checkable:


```
  1. the password string (not the hash of the result)
  2. the exact openssl command, including -md
```


Then anyone can run it. If it produces 4f7a1e4e I'll say so publicly and drop this.

I'm not claiming anyone acted in bad faith. jackdevs66's XOR key genuinely is correct, and I
think this spread because that part checks out and people reasonably assumed the rest did too.
But right now the anchor a lot of us are measuring against can't be regenerated from any public
artifact, and that's worth knowing before more months go into it.

Happy to be wrong. Show me the command.

[#68259] 15:27:19 MrNobody (user6789043700)
Correction: I was wrong. @rickluminari1 derivation reproduces 4f7a1e4e exactly. Verified on my side.

What I got wrong: the password is the 32 RAW BINARY bytes, not the 64-character hex string. I
ran -pass pass:a795de11... which passes the hex as text. The correct form is
bytes.fromhex('a795de11...') used directly as the password, with the MD5 KDF. Ran his code as
posted, got 4f7a1e4efe4bf6c5581e32505c019657cb7b030e90232d33f011aca6a5e9c081. Match.

So I retract the claim that the checkpoint can't be produced from the published method. It can.
It's reproducible and that part of the record is sound. If anyone was told their bytes were
wrong on the strength of my post, that was my error, not theirs.

Annoying detail for me: the rule I broke is one I already knew. Always test the raw phrase, the
sha-hex string, and the raw digest bytes. I tested two of three and published as if I'd tested
all of them. That's on me.

One thing I'd genuinely like to understand, and I'm asking, not arguing:

The derivation needs -md md5. Every solved phase in this puzzle needs -md sha256 and breaks
under md5. Control I re-ran just now, phase 3.2 with its known password:


```
-md sha256  -> 2422 bytes, "I've been waiting for you. You have many questions..."
-md md5     -> PKCS7 invalid, fails outright
```


So the chain is sha256 at every verified step, and this one step is md5. That's the bit I can't
place.

Two things that might explain it and I have no way to choose between them:

1. The author changed KDF for this stage, and the 1327 bytes are a further encrypted or packed
   layer, which is why they look random (entropy 7.87 of 8, incompressible, printable 0.389).

2. The key is wrong and landed valid padding by luck. I measured that: random 32-byte keys give
   valid PKCS7 on this blob 63 times in 20000, about 1 in 317. With the four password/KDF
   combinations, plus the different 7-token sets people have tried (issue #56 uses another one),
   one landing valid isn't a remarkable event.

I don't think 1 or 2 can be settled by staring at the bytes. What would settle it is anything
downstream that only works if the 1327 bytes are correct. If the 103x103 matrix work produces
something that checks against an independent anchor, that's the answer and I'll shut up lol.

Either way, the reproducibility question is closed and Rick was right. Thanks for posting the
code instead of just telling me I was wrong,

[#68284] 17:14:00 MrNobody (user6789043700)
I tried the checkerboard reading, which is the author's own method from phase 3.2. If dbbi
encodes a 64-char hex digest then exactly one prefix set works, {b,g}, parsing it into exactly
64 tokens over exactly 16 slots. faed gives no valid hex reading at any prefix count.

Then I brute forced the mapping. 16 slots onto 16 hex chars is 16! = 20,922,789,888,000. Ran the
whole space twice, the second pass making no assumption about plaintext length or
content. 41.8 trillion trials, 13 GPU hours, zero hits.

So it's closed, don't spend a night on it 😪

One thing worth knowing though. The "dbbi/faed are proven noise" result only tests for LANGUAGE.
I checked: take a random sha256 hex digest, encode it with a 9-column checkerboard, and it
passes all ten of those statistical tests. So the honest reading is "no readable language in
there", not "nothing in there". Different claim.

@B58MBU0  before hour 132 on the xor triangle, one verifiable thing worth 5 min: every confirmed stage decrypts with openssl -md sha256. the cosmic blob is the only one that "works" with -md md5, and even then the 7 token key is the single combo that lands valid PKCS7. run it with -md sha256 (the method that cracked every other stage) and it's a bad decrypt. so the 1327 byte output isn't a real decryption under the puzzle's own consistent method, it's a padding hit. @CoruNethron tried it. base b1 -> reverse -> base b2, iterated up to 5 rounds, every base pair from 2 to 36. best printable ratio 0.77, no text. nested base+reverse doesn't crack it either. worth refining if you meant something more specific. @kamsqe on your "falsifiable check" question, i think the check is that faed shouldn't decode to text at all. its index of coincidence is ~0.118, flat, random for a 9-symbol alphabet, and it gives zero readable output across every base mapping. the block is statistically not text-encoded. so any decode that produces english (the triangle, witveen, whatever) is by definition reading structure into noise. that flips the criterion: a correct faed decode should yield data that verifies by USE, not readability. a value whose hash hits a known anchor, or key material that opens the next blob, or bytes with a real signature. not a word. if we accept that, "find the english phrase" was always the wrong target, and everyone stuck at a yin-yang is stuck because they're looking for meaning in a block that was never text.

Assuming that some manual modifications were intentionally made to AES Cosmic, string 4 stands out.


> In a typical 64-character Base64 string, a roughly equal number of uppercase and lowercase letters is expected—around 26/26.


Consider string 4:

SATSFO7IFBiAMz7dDqIETKuGlTAP4EmMQUZrQNtfbJsURATW6V5VSbtZB5RFk0O+

It contains approximately: 41 uppercase letters, 15 lowercase letters, 7 digits
The bias toward uppercase letters is quite strong, and this is also visually noticeable.

I’ve gone through your research, and I think it definitely deserves attention. But I have a slightly different view on the AES stage.

My feeling is that trying to decrypt the AES before fully solving the DBBI section may be too early. By doing that, we could be losing a large amount of information that might actually serve as instructions rather than just intermediate data.

My current theory is that the words you get while solving the entire SalPh stage are meant to tell you how to construct the AES password. So it may not be only about finding the final candidate, but also understanding what the previous layers tell us to do with it — for example:

SHA256(candidate) → AES password

So I think it may make more sense to fully reconstruct the DBBI/SalPh logic first, and only then use the AES as a validation of that path.

The DBBIB prime-token rail (16 B / 7 BE) is the low bit of each ASCII character of 
gsmg.io/theseedisplanted, with JRK's {1},{4},{21} applied as marker indices set ON, truncated to 23 bits.

parity of the URL : 111101110011110110010010
markers 1 and 4 are already 1; marker 21 is 0 → set it
first 23 bits     : 11110111001111011001101   = the DBBIB mask

So {1},{4},{21} is a board correction, not a word index, two of the three are already satisfied, and the third is exactly the bit that has to flip.

Fair challenge🤔... and no, I'm not asserting it as fact. It's an inference. Here's how strong it is.

Certain: the blob is 96 bytes (16 of Salted__ + salt, then 80 bytes of ciphertext equals 5 AES blocks). Under AES-CBC with PKCS7 that pins the plaintext to 64 to 79 bytes. That's arithmetic, not opinion.

Why I said 64 lowercase hex: 64 is the floor of that range and a 64-char hex string pads to exactly 80; the page's own shabefanstoo reads as "sha before, answer too"; and 64 lowercase hex is both the shape of every password in this chain and the shape of a raw private key.

Where you're right: the solved plaintexts in this puzzle have been documents, not bare digests (phase 3.2 decrypts to 2,422 bytes of prose with a nested blob inside it). So "each plaintext is just the next password" isn't actually the established pattern here. I should have said 64 to 79 bytes, with 64-hex the most likely single form, not "exactly". Correcting that.

What it doesn't change: the ask. Post SHA256 of whatever your plaintext is (64 hex chars, 70 bytes of prose, a WIF, doesn't matter). The commitment is format-agnostic; that's the point of it.

And one thing your challenge is worth, concretely: I'd been using "plaintext is exactly 64 hex" as a fast filter in my own searching (which would silently miss a 65 to 79 byte plaintext). I'm re-running with a printability test on every candidate that produces valid padding instead. If that's the error you were flagging🚩 it was a real one🙏

Request for original GSMG / SalPhaseIon records

I am not asking the creator for another hint or for the private key. I am trying to recover the historical record of one unresolved attachment in SalPhaseIon.

The page mechanically gives:

`SHA256 OUR FIRST HINT IS YOUR LAST COMMAND`

followed by an OpenSSL `Salted__` object. The surviving transcript contains this important exchange:

> `pls... is salph related to hint about "roses are..."?`  
> Creator's next message: `Hush hush`

That strongly links SalPhase to the official “Roses are White…” hint, whose final line is `Hush hush.` Another preserved creator reply supports returning to the first puzzle image and hashing its visible text. What remains missing is the exact attachment: whether SHA-256 takes the literal hint, its final command, the first-image text, the result of executing the command, or the preceding answer labelled `THISPASSWORD`.

If anyone has original material from roughly 2019–2021, I would appreciate any of the following:

1. a raw Telegram or Discord export containing the March 14–15, 2021 SalPhase / `Hush hush` exchange, including message IDs, `reply_to` metadata, and edit timestamps;
2. a pre-edit copy or screenshot of creator message 1710 containing the complete January 2020 hint;
3. an HTML response, server/source archive, screenshot, or downloaded asset from the SalPhaseIon page earlier than May 2023;
4. any creator-authored file or message that explicitly identifies the SHA-256 input, password serialization, OpenSSL command, or IV handling;
5. a record defining the page suffix `SHABEFANSTOO`.

Please preserve files exactly as received. Useful verification information includes the filename, byte length, SHA-256 checksum, original date, source group/channel, and message/reply identifiers. Even a record that disproves the proposed connection would be useful.

What has already been checked:

- all five distinct successful Wayback HTML variants preserve both puzzle textareas byte-for-byte;
- the page has no hidden fields, comments, puzzle scripts, linked assets, or historical IV field;
- the obvious exact forms of `HUSH`, `HUSH HUSH`, the complete formal hint, the rabbit wording, the first-image text, its known route hash, and the archived image bytes do not open the small object under the established OpenSSL models;
- the object authenticates an 8-byte salt, not a separate 16-byte IV.

The aim is to restore missing provenance, not to generate more unconstrained password guesses.

[#69800] 16:56:17 Thiago Santos (user8643841352)
(reply to #69798 - Loupi (user2104527981): "It should be there now. I’m not sure if I put it in the r...")
(edited 2026-08-24 17:24:39)
(reactions: 🙏 x1)
Same decode here, byte-for-byte: `sha256(output)[:8] = 15d62c82`, starting `btcseeddeoemckeadhbschdkbdcsdkdv…`

Small note that may save others a step: your 9-letter `DBIFHCEGA` and the 8-letter `DBIFHCEG` produce the identical square, since `a` is the next unused letter alphabetically either way.

On the single `z` — I ran a null and I think it's mechanical rather than planted.

`FAED` uses only `a`–`i`, i.e. square indices 0–8, so rows ∈ {0,1} and cols ∈ {0..4}. After fractionation and re-reading in pairs, even output positions get two *row* values (only `d,b,c,e` possible) and odd positions get two *col* values (anything possible). `z` = square[24] = (4,4), so it needs two consecutive col-4s, and col 4 comes from `e` — which occurs 69 times (12.1%) in FAED.

Shuffling FAED 3000× and re-running the same Bifid:


```
mean #z = 2.89     P(#z == 1) = 14.2%     P(#z >= 1) = 95.8%
```


So one `z` isn't rare. And conditioned on exactly one, its position lands in the first half 50.6% of the time — no signal there either.

The even/odd split above may be the more productive grain: it's the same alternation that splits the 563 into the two channels people have been working on. Your `90 | z | 472` cut runs across it.

Nice writeup either way. The reproducibility is the valuable part.

[#69850] 21:28:41 Suppa (user768637046)
Hi all. I've been working through the GSMG 5 BTC puzzle from the public material (Naddiseo's repo + the hint screenshots) and I've hit the same wall everyone seems to hit at SalPhaseIon. Before I burn more time, a few questions for people who've been here longer.

First, something I found that I haven't seen written up anywhere, in case it's useful or in case someone already knows about it:

The Decentraland puzzlepiece.mp3 has content in the side channel. Left and right are each plain white noise, but L-R contains a deliberate periodic signal: period exactly 684 samples at 44.1 kHz (64.4737 Hz), odd harmonics only, and it is half-wave antisymmetric — avg[k] = -avg[k+342], correlation 0.9997. I ruled out a joint-stereo codec artifact with a control: same bitrate, same encoder, same channel correlation on synthetic noise gives autocorrelation 0.002 at lag 683 versus 0.837 for the real file. It carries no modulation (no FSK/PSK/AM — phase residual 1.6 degrees, no phase jumps), so as far as I can tell the only payload is the parameters themselves.

My questions:

Is that mp3 side-channel signal known? The 2021-02-12 summary in the group said "blobs in mp3 didn't recovered" — did anyone ever get anything out of it, and what were the blobs people expected to find?

Jrk said "once you hit a 'ying yang', you'll be able to solve it the same day." Half-wave antisymmetry is literally 180-degree rotational antisymmetry. Is that what the ying yang is, or is it a different object entirely? Has anyone found an object in the puzzle with that property?

primes: the Architect text says "reinserting the prime basics", and Jrk confirmed prime numbers are "required to proceed" plus "some characters need to be zeroed out". Is the community's reading that this is positional (characters at prime indices) or that 2/3/5/7 are values to insert? And reinserted into what object?

dbbib (91 symbols) and the 570-symbol faed head: the z-separated tail decodes cleanly with a=1..i=9, o=0 into decimal -> int -> hex -> ASCII, giving lastwordsbeforearchichoice and thispassword. The 91 and the 570 don't decode under the same rule. Has anyone got anything past the Bifid step on those two, or is that still open?

lastwordsbeforearchichoice — what exact string does the group treat as the answer? I've tried every contiguous substring of the decoded Architect text and none of them open anything.

The 80-byte AES blob at the very end of phase 3.2 (salt b45a5e3d): any progress on it at all since 2019, or is it universally still closed?

Not asking anyone to hand over work — happy to share anything I find. Thanks.

file — ranked 1, 2, 3 out of 196 for L−R energy below 7 kHz. The picture
is at its loudest exactly there, so LAME's stereo decision dropped MS for
those frames. With MS off, L and R get quantized independently and their
HF noise stops cancelling. That's the entire anomaly.

Not a payload:
- carrier phase runs continuous through all 3, no splice
- the 3 HF residuals don't correlate with each other (.03 / .00 / .07)
- broadband 7–22k, ~85 peaks each, no tonal structure

[#69862] 23:55:03 Suppa (user768637046)
(reply to #69857 - n04oh (user5386650593): "Lmao I did some calculations")
n04oh's number is basically right. Derivation:

In the Bifid output, even positions can only be b/c/d/e (row values) and
odd positions can be any of 25 (col values). btcseed = b·t·c·s·e·e·d is
4 even + 3 odd, so

  uniform:                 (1/4)^4 × (1/25)^3  = 1 in 4,000,000
  observed letter freqs:                        1 in 3,861,733

Same order as his 2.5M. Not false.

But the 24-word mnemonic people pull out of the BCDE channel is a
separate claim, and that one doesn't hold. The channel is 282 symbols,
you need 132 contiguous, so 151 offsets × 24 possible 2-bit mappings =
3,624 trials, each with a 1/256 checksum. Expectation: 14.2.

I ran all 3,624. Exactly 13 give a valid BIP39 checksum. The known one
(offset 27, d=00 c=01 b=10 e=11) is one of those 13. A valid checksum
here carries no evidence at all.

And it's empty on chain — BIP44/49/84, external and internal, indexes
0–2, all 18 addresses: 0 transactions, never funded.

btcseed itself is probably real signal. The mnemonic derived from it is
noise.

[#69863] 23:56:21 Suppa (user768637046)
(reply to #69858 - B58 (user6636122506): "yes i know you are llm power user, what's the calculation...")
Fair objection, and it's the right one — look-elsewhere. I quoted the
probability of a pre-specified string, but nobody specified it in
advance. So I measured the correction instead of arguing about it.

The structure constrains it hard: even positions can only be b/c/d/e,
odd positions any of 25. Of the 23,881 seven-letter words in
/usr/share/dict/words, exactly 40 fit that pattern — bicycle, debacle,
cubicle, decided, cudweed, eyeseed, and 34 more.

  pre-specified "btcseed":      1 in 4,000,000
  any English dictionary word:  1 in 100,000

So your correction is 40x, not 4,000,000x. And none of those 40 is
crypto-relevant. btcseed is the only domain term I could build that
fits — privkey, seedkey, keyseed, bitcoin all fail the pattern.
(dadless fails too, position 6 would have to be b/c/d/e. The pattern
is stricter than it looks, which is exactly why the correction is small.)

I'd put btcseed nearer the 4M end than the 100k end. But you're right
that 4M isn't the honest number to quote.

On "nothing is provable on both sides until the end" — one side is.
The 24-word mnemonic people pull out of the BCDE channel: 282 symbols,
132 needed contiguous, 151 offsets × 24 mappings = 3,624 trials at
1/256 each. Expectation 14.2 valid checksums. I ran all 3,624: exactly
13. The known one (offset 27, d=00 c=01 b=10 e=11) is one of the 13.
All 18 addresses across BIP44/49/84, ext+int, indexes 0–2: zero
transactions, never funded.

btcseed may well be real. The mnemonic downstream of it is chance.
